assumptions.summary: Cyclists and bicycles are represented as particles over a 20-40 km course.
Sharp turns are assumed flat and riders move uniformly through them.
Riders of the same gender use one average mass.
Human energy-supply processes use constant rates despite biochemical complexity.
All six team riders have the same or similar physical quality.
Pull handovers ignore retreat time, acceleration, deceleration, and position changes.
Followers use 75 percent of the leader's aerodynamic resistance.
Team pulls on curves and hills are treated like straight-road pulls.

contributions.summary: Order the paper from bioenergetics through mechanics, strategy, application, diagnostics, and team guidance.

Produce gender- and type-specific theoretical power profiles from one energy model.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Online reference curves provide four characteristic powers for male/female comparisons, but the raw sample is not packaged.
Table 2 supplies mass and energy-system parameters for male/female time-trial specialists.
Table 4 supplies corresponding parameters for male/female sprinters.
The self-designed route combines straights, ramps, 90-degree turns, and 180-degree turns.
Tokyo is reconstructed from an official roadmap with a reported 4.5 percent length error.
Flanders is reconstructed at 43.0 km versus an actual 43.3 km route.
Table 6 provides four rider-profile finish times for Tokyo, Belgium, and the designed course.
A male specialist on the designed course is recomputed over wind direction and speed conditions.

models.summary: Eq.1-Eq.6 aggregate component power, deplete CP, cap ATP-CP production, and restore CP.
Eq.7-Eq.10 couple oxygen and lactate states, production/decomposition rates, and physiological caps.
Eq.11-Eq.12 and Figure 4 define a branching supply controller with a lactate-threshold penalty.
Eq.13-Eq.16 define quadratic aerodynamic force, grade force, rolling force, and slope-adjusted normal force.
Eq.17-Eq.19 combine eta P=Fv with translational and wheel rotational energy.
Eq.20-Eq.22 relate lean angle, centripetal demand, friction, and vmax=sqrt(gRk).
Figure 11 and Eq.23 compare variable-speed work with a constant-speed baseline and route exceptions by terrain.
Eq.24-Eq.29 decompose wind, evolve heading, and integrate mean drag for pi/2 and pi turns.
Eq.30-Eq.32 use full versus 75 percent drag, T1>=5T0, and a four-rider finish-distance constraint.

results_trace.summary: gender-profile comparison: four duration powers -> male/female curves -> larger short-duration gap. Boundary: Report the underlying samples and uncertainty before generalizing by gender.
specialist-curve result: parameter set -> component curves -> total male/female specialist profiles. Boundary: Keep theoretical curves separate from measured validation data.
sprinter-curve result: sprinter parameters -> higher explosive branch -> male/female profiles. Boundary: Type labels require empirical classification criteria.
theoretical-curves-to-decision: theoretical curves -> real-world resemblance -> reliability claim -> strategy use. Boundary: Visual resemblance is a plausibility check, not independent validation.
three-course finish-time result: rider profile + course -> simulated time -> cross-profile comparison. Boundary: Every result inherits route reconstruction and parameter uncertainty.
modeled-53.02-to-decision: modeled 53.02 -> actual 53.02? -> model claim. Boundary: Clarify the actual benchmark and avoid circular or mismatched comparisons.
modeled-53.02/57.41-to-decision: modeled 53.02/57.41 -> champion 57.78 -> closeness claim. Boundary: Use a consistent reported modeled time across Summary and body.

power-speed-position interpretation: road conditions -> target power -> speed response -> rider-quality difference. Boundary: A simulated controller following its own policy is not behavioral validation.

execution-deviation result: target-power perturbation -> finish time -> percentage change -> practical robustness. Boundary: Define each deviation trajectory; the signs and combined plus/minus rows are not interchangeable.
weather-time result: wind direction/speed -> completion time -> course symmetry interpretation. Boundary: Retain the course-specific geometry and wind grid.
team-speed result: pull/recovery strategy -> normal-phase gain 14.43% -> sprint gain 18.52%. Boundary: Report baseline, solver, distance, and fourth-rider timing before operational use.

power-profile-regions-to-decision: power-profile regions -> rider classification -> terrain and team actions. Boundary: Separate model-derived guidance from coaching extensions not computed in the paper.

weaknesses.summary: Eq.1-Eq.12 lack complete units and calibrated state values for ATP, CP, lactate, oxygen, and conversion efficiencies.
The coupled glycolysis-aerobic system uses symbols and caps whose initial values and numerical update rules are incomplete.
Figure 4's branch controller does not fully specify simultaneous depletion, restoration, or nonnegative-state safeguards.
The gender and rider-type profile comparisons omit raw observations, sample sizes, fitted uncertainty, and holdout validation.
The model calls a visual resemblance to reference curves proof of reliability without a quantitative validation metric.
Eq.13 uses ground speed in baseline aerodynamic drag, while wind-relative speed is introduced only later.
The drivetrain efficiency statement uses about 0.95, but notation and subsequent equations do not consistently preserve it.
Eq.17 has a v=0 singularity and the motion solve omits braking and numerical integration details.
Eq.20-Eq.22 do not document the exact lean/friction geometry or wet-road calibration.
The fixed-speed optimality argument compares an incompletely defined class of strategies and does not solve a full optimal-control problem.
Tokyo and Flanders route reconstruction uses image geometry but publishes no coordinates, segmentation code, or error propagation.
The Summary's Belgium modeled time and the body/table values are not presented consistently enough to identify one authoritative benchmark.
Figure 15 is generated by the model following its own controller and therefore is internal consistency, not external behavioral validation.
Table 7 mixes negative and plus/minus deviation scenarios without defining their power trajectories, sampling, or work normalization.
Eq.24-Eq.29 have an unclear wind sign convention and no independent vector-aerodynamic validation.
The weather experiment omits the exact wind grid and uncertainty; rain is discussed without numerical friction data.
The 75 percent drafting coefficient is not calibrated by spacing, rider order, yaw, or a primary source.
The team model assumes homogeneous riders and instantaneous handovers, which can overstate recovery and speed gains.
Eq.32 has ambiguous indices, units, distance closure, and objective; the optimizer and feasibility checks are absent.
The 14.43 and 18.52 percent team gains cannot be reproduced from disclosed trajectories or fourth-rider timing.
The guidance recommends braking in turns despite the body strategy/turn assumption relying on uniform motion and omitted braking dynamics.
Several references are web sources without access dates, and the exact data borrowed from them is not identified.
Extracted text contains encoding corruption; rendered 200-DPI pages are authoritative for equations and typography.
Eq.4 is inconsistent with Eq.3: the printed expression uses remaining CP content where integrating the depletion equation requires consumed content M_CP-V_CP(t).
Eq.23 leaves a and f insufficiently tied to prior parameters and cannot establish constant speed as globally optimal; Section 10.1.2 itself concedes the strategy analysis is incomplete.
Eq.24 and Eq.30-Eq.31 use mu in the mechanical power balance even though Eq.17 defines drivetrain efficiency eta and Eq.1 reserves mu for ATP-energy conversion.
Expanding Eq.26 over a turn indicates Eq.28 should contain vx^2+vy^2 rather than vx^2-vy^2, and Eq.29 omits the mean 0.5(vx^2+vy^2) term.
Weather conclusions use one male specialist, one designed course, and deterministic wind cases; significance language has no statistical design or error bound.
Eq.32 reuses V for team speed and physical-strength units and switches U0/U1 in prose to u0/u1 in the formula.
The drafting discussion cites resistance as low as two thirds, then assumes 75 percent without rationale or coefficient sensitivity.
The Belgium simulation is faster than the champion time, yet the body calls it inferior; even after route-length adjustment the modeled mean speed remains higher.
The Tokyo champion average speed is printed as 13 km/h, while 21.1 km in 28.10 minutes implies about 45.05 km/h or 12.51 m/s.
The Summary's 30 percent deviation and 3.11 percent result refers only to the mixed plus/minus 30 percent row; fixed -30 percent produces a 7.76 percent time change.
The Summary's 14.43 percent team improvement applies only to the normal pull phase, while the body separately reports 18.52 percent for the sprint phase.

Several visual references and captions are mismatched: p10 points to Tables 4/5 instead of 2/3, p20 shifts Figures 17/18, Figure 16 is captioned as a course, and Figure 20 repeats an Individual Time Trial caption.
